overview.headline: Radioactive waste types, hazards, storage, disposal and decay

keyPoints.point: There are two broad classifications of radioactive waste into high level and low level types
keyPoints.quote: There are two broad classifications: high-level or low-level waste.

keyPoints.point: Fission products account for most heat and penetrating radiation in high level waste
keyPoints.quote: These isotopes, called "fission products," account for most of the heat and penetrating radiation in high-level waste.

keyPoints.point: Strontium and cesium have half-lives of about thirty years and half the radioactivity will decay in that time
keyPoints.quote: Strontium-90 and cesium-137 have half-lives of about 30 years (half the radioactivity will decay in 30 years).

keyPoints.point: Water in spent fuel pools serves to shield radiation and cool rods before transfer to casks
keyPoints.quote: The water is typically about 40 feet deep and serves both to shield the radiation and cool the rods.

keyTerms.gloss: isotopes that account for most heat and penetrating radiation from fuel
keyTerms.quote: These isotopes, called "fission products," account for most of the heat and penetrating radiation in high-level waste.

keyTerms.gloss: hazard remaining in high level waste after long time from heavier elements
keyTerms.quote: Transuranic wastes, sometimes called TRU, account for most of the radioactive hazard remaining in high-level waste after 1,000 years.

keyTerms.gloss: time in years for half the amount to decay
keyTerms.quote: Plutonium-239 has a half-life of 24,000 years.

keyTerms.gloss: uranium fuel removed from reactors after producing electricity that is thermally hot
keyTerms.quote: High-level waste is primarily spent fuel removed from reactors after producing electricity.

keyTerms.gloss: concrete surrounded canister used for storage of cooled fuel from pools
keyTerms.quote: As the pools near capacity, utilities move some of the older spent fuel into “dry cask” storage.
